## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. 11	
12	Cynefin (pronounced "kuh-NEV-in") is a sensemaking framework created by Dave Snowden. It helps us recognize that different kinds of problems need fundamentally different approaches. It has four main domains: Clear, Complicated, Complex, and Chaotic.
13	
14	![](../images/323595-framework-scaled-1024x1024-1-600x600-1.png)
15	
16	### Clear (formerly Simple/Obvious)
17	
18	In my CSM classes, I teach Cynefin using examples from everyday life. I start by asking: "How many of you know how to change the batteries in a flashlight?" Most hands go up. "What about the batteries in your car remote?" A few hands drop. "What about changing a tire on your car?" A few more drop.
19	
20	These are all examples of Clear problems. The relationship between cause and effect is obvious. You sense the problem, categorize it based on what you already know (or can easily learn), and respond using a known best practice. Once you have learned the solution, it stays learned.
21	
22	### Complicated
23	
24	Next I ask: "Can you take apart your car engine and put it back together?" Almost nobody can. But a trained mechanic can, because they know the sequence - take it apart step by step, then reassemble in roughly the reverse order.
25	
26	This is a Complicated problem. It is made up of many Clear steps done in sequence, but you need expertise or analysis to figure out the right sequence. The approach is: sense the problem, analyze it (get expert help, watch videos, create a plan), then respond. The traditional waterfall model works well here because the problem is knowable in advance - you just need to do the analysis first.
27	
28	### Complex
29	
30	Then I ask: "How long does it take you to commute to work?" Everyone shares an estimate. "Does it always take that long?" No. "What changes?" Road conditions, weather, accidents, construction, car trouble.
31	
32	This is a Complex problem. The underlying conditions are always shifting, so cause and effect can only be understood in hindsight. Product development works the same way - requirements change, technology evolves, and what the customer wants today may not be what they want next month.
33	
34	For Complex problems, you need a framework built for change. Scrum is exactly that. It keeps work transparent, inspects results frequently, and adapts based on what the team learns. You cannot plan your way to a solution - you have to probe, sense what happens, and respond.
35	
36	### Chaotic
37	
38	Imagine driving in a country where nobody follows traffic laws. Cars run red lights, drive on whichever side of the road they feel like, and pedestrians walk wherever they want. That is Chaos - there is no relationship between cause and effect that you can discover in time to be useful.
39	
40	In Chaos, you act first to stabilize the situation, then sense what is happening, then respond. The priority is to move out of Chaos and into one of the other domains as quickly as possible.
41	
42	### Why This Matters
43	
44	Most organizations are tackling Complex problems but using approaches designed for the Complicated domain (detailed upfront plans, Gantt charts, fixed scope). Cynefin helps explain why those approaches keep failing and why frameworks like Scrum - built around short feedback loops and adaptation - are a better fit.

Cynefin is hard to wrap your head around. It took me over two years to start to get it. But once you do, it changes how you see problems - and why certain approaches work in some situations and fail in others.

Cynefin (pronounced "kuh-NEV-in") is a sensemaking framework created by Dave Snowden. It helps us recognize that different kinds of problems need fundamentally different approaches. It has four main domains: Clear, Complicated, Complex, and Chaotic.

![](../images/323595-framework-scaled-1024x1024-1-600x600-1.png)

### Clear (formerly Simple/Obvious)

In my CSM classes, I teach Cynefin using examples from everyday life. I start by asking: "How many of you know how to change the batteries in a flashlight?" Most hands go up. "What about the batteries in your car remote?" A few hands drop. "What about changing a tire on your car?" A few more drop.

These are all examples of Clear problems. The relationship between cause and effect is obvious. You sense the problem, categorize it based on what you already know (or can easily learn), and respond using a known best practice. Once you have learned the solution, it stays learned.

### Complicated

Next I ask: "Can you take apart your car engine and put it back together?" Almost nobody can. But a trained mechanic can, because they know the sequence - take it apart step by step, then reassemble in roughly the reverse order.

This is a Complicated problem. It is made up of many Clear steps done in sequence, but you need expertise or analysis to figure out the right sequence. The approach is: sense the problem, analyze it (get expert help, watch videos, create a plan), then respond. The traditional waterfall model works well here because the problem is knowable in advance - you just need to do the analysis first.

### Complex

Then I ask: "How long does it take you to commute to work?" Everyone shares an estimate. "Does it always take that long?" No. "What changes?" Road conditions, weather, accidents, construction, car trouble.

This is a Complex problem. The underlying conditions are always shifting, so cause and effect can only be understood in hindsight. Product development works the same way - requirements change, technology evolves, and what the customer wants today may not be what they want next month.

For Complex problems, you need a framework built for change. Scrum is exactly that. It keeps work transparent, inspects results frequently, and adapts based on what the team learns. You cannot plan your way to a solution - you have to probe, sense what happens, and respond.

### Chaotic

Imagine driving in a country where nobody follows traffic laws. Cars run red lights, drive on whichever side of the road they feel like, and pedestrians walk wherever they want. That is Chaos - there is no relationship between cause and effect that you can discover in time to be useful.

In Chaos, you act first to stabilize the situation, then sense what is happening, then respond. The priority is to move out of Chaos and into one of the other domains as quickly as possible.

### Why This Matters

Most organizations are tackling Complex problems but using approaches designed for the Complicated domain (detailed upfront plans, Gantt charts, fixed scope). Cynefin helps explain why those approaches keep failing and why frameworks like Scrum - built around short feedback loops and adaptation - are a better fit.

For a deeper explanation, see: [Complexity](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/complexity)

### Assignment

Share your learnings from the Cynefin model in about 100 words in your personal Mural board. In particular, consider: which domain does most of the work in your organization fall into, and does the approach your organization uses match that domain?

Before we dig into tools for resolving organizational impediments, take a few minutes to reflect on your own experience.

- What are the biggest impediments you face as a Scrum Master?
- Which of those are within your team's control, and which are organizational?
- Have you tried to resolve any of them? What happened?

Jot down your answers - you will use them in the assignment below.

### Resolving an Organizational Impediment

Now pick the organizational impediment that has the most impact on your team's ability to deliver. Your goal is to work on it with the people who can actually change it. Here are two techniques that work well for surfacing and acting on organizational impediments.

### TRIZ / "What Would Make Things Worse?"

Ask the group: "What could we do to guarantee this impediment never gets resolved?" Then invert the answers.

This technique comes from Liberating Structures and works well with mixed groups of team members and stakeholders because it is non-threatening. People laugh while listing the worst ideas, and in the process they often surface political or structural truths that nobody would say directly. Once you have the "worst ideas" list, flip each one: "We said we'd guarantee failure by hiding the problem from leadership - so what would it look like to make it visible?"

### Impediment Board Review

If your team does not already have a visible impediment backlog, introduce one. Create a simple board (physical or digital) listing every known impediment. Then review each item with stakeholders:

- Is it stale? Should it be removed or updated?
- Who owns it? Is there a named person responsible for the next action?
- What is the next concrete step?

Stakeholders who see this list often feel more accountability when impediments are explicit and visible rather than buried in meeting notes or forgotten backlogs.

### Using GenAI to Deepen Your Analysis

Once you have identified an impediment, you can use generative AI as a thinking partner to explore it from a systems perspective. See [Using GenAI and Systems Thinking for Team Problems](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/genai-systems-thinking-team-problems/) for a practical guide to using AI prompts that help you map causes, feedback loops, and unintended consequences.

### Assignment

1. Identify an organizational impediment in your organization.
2. Use one of the techniques above (TRIZ or Impediment Board Review) to explore it with stakeholders.
3. Use [Systems Thinking](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/systems-thinking/) either the old fashioned way or with an LLM to deepen your understanding.
4. Answer the following questions and share them in your personal Mural board:
    - **What would be the first change?** (short-term win)
    - **What gets in the way of action on that?** (barriers)
    - **What would the next step be?** (build on the change)
    - **How would you make it stick?**

In 8.1, you explored the coaching stances and applied them to solve a team impediment. Now it is time to go deeper: applying specific coaching techniques in two distinct situations and then analyzing what worked and what you would improve.

### Assignment
#### Part 1: Two Coaching Interventions

Choose two different situations with your team or organization where you will apply a coaching technique. The two situations should be meaningfully different from each other - for example, one might be a one-on-one conversation and the other a team-level intervention.

For each intervention, document:
1. **The situation** - What was happening? Who was involved?
2. **The coaching technique you chose** - Which stance or approach did you use? (e.g., maintaining neutrality, powerful questions, facilitative listening, serving the client's agenda, not colluding)
3. **Why you chose it** - What made this technique appropriate for this situation?
4. **What happened** - How did the person or team respond? What was the outcome?

#### Part 2: Analyzing Your Interventions
After completing both interventions, step back and reflect on each one:

For each intervention, identify at least two things you would do differently next time. Consider:
- Did you stay in a coaching stance, or did you slip into advising or directing?
- Was your timing right, or would the intervention have landed better at a different moment?
- Did you choose the right coaching technique for the situation, or would a different approach have been more effective?
- Were there signals from the other person or team that you missed or misread?
- Did you reduce dependence, or did you inadvertently create more reliance on yourself?

Write up both interventions and your analysis in 400-600 words total. Share this on your personal Mural board.

title: "3.2B Diagnosing TIA Failures"
status: published
slug: "a-csm/section-3-service-to-the-organization/3.2b-diagnosing-tia-failures"

tableOfContents: false

In 3.2 you saw why Complex problems need a framework built around transparency, inspection, and adaptation (TIA). Scrum's empirical process control depends on all three working together - if one breaks down, the whole loop breaks down, and the team stops actually learning from its work.

Knowing the theory is one thing. Recognizing TIA failure when you are standing inside it is another. Each pillar fails in its own characteristic way:

### Transparency Failures

The information the team and stakeholders need is missing, hidden, or misleading. A Definition of Done that nobody enforces, a Sprint Backlog that does not reflect what people are actually working on, or a status report that says "on track" when it is not - these all rob everyone of a shared, honest picture of reality. Without transparency, inspection has nothing real to look at.

### Inspection Failures

The right information exists, but nobody looks at it closely enough, often enough, or at all. A Sprint Review that turns into a demo with no real feedback, a Daily Scrum that becomes a status report to the Scrum Master instead of a working session for the Developers, or a Retrospective that surfaces the same issues every time with no one checking whether last time's insight actually held up - these are all inspection breaking down.

### Adaptation Failures

The team inspects, sees a problem, and does nothing about it. Maybe nobody has the authority to change course. Maybe the organization punishes teams for changing plans. Maybe the team has simply stopped believing that raising the issue again will change anything. Adaptation failures are often the most demoralizing, because the team did the work of sensing the problem and still could not act on it.

### Assignment

Identify three situations, past or present, where transparency, inspection, or adaptation was not working effectively. They can come from the same team or different teams, and you do not need to have been the Scrum Master at the time.

For each situation, answer:

1. **Which pillar failed** - transparency, inspection, or adaptation? (More than one may apply - if so, say which one broke down first.)
2. **What happened** - describe the situation concretely enough that someone outside the team would understand it.
3. **Why it failed** - was it a skills gap, a structural/organizational barrier, a trust issue, or something else?
4. **What you would change** - what is one concrete step that would have restored that pillar?

Share your three situations and analysis in about 300-400 words on your personal Mural board.

### Assignment
Arlen, a technical architect, and Shilpa, a program manager, are jointly responsible for delivery of a credit approval software product. They both report to the same managing director, Chidi. The product needs to incorporate a workflow tool to orchestrate the different steps and collaborations needed for credit approval. Chidi got permission from his management and the product owner to build the workflow tool instead of buying one.

It has been six months. The developers are working on the workflow tool and have not been able to incorporate any business functionality or begin building the product. When will the workflow tool be ready remains unclear. The business and the product owner are getting impatient.

Sensing this, Shilpa set up a call with their managing director, Chidi, Arlen and herself.

In that discussion, Arlen's explanation is that they are using Agile and Scrum to build this workflow tool. In his view, according to the Agile values, both plans and documentation are not required as they've demonstrated the workflow tool and proved that it works. They merely need more time to start using it.

Shilpa points out the business need: a credit approval product. She asks for an estimated date for how much more time is needed, both for the workflow tool and the product needed by the business. Arlen is reluctant to give even a ballpark range.

Seeking alternatives, Shilpa asks about buying a workflow tool instead. After some discussion, Arlen increasingly attempts to shift the focus back to what the team has demonstrated and away from outside tools.

Chidi begins to glare a bit. He revives the underlying business need for a credit approval product. Arlen digs in his heels as his voice volume grows a notch, advocating to continue iterations to build the workflow tool. Chidi and Shilpa continue to press their business point with growing vigor. With 15 minutes remaining in the meeting, and tension growing, Arlen suddenly mentions a conflicting call and drops off the call.

Read the Scenario  and Answer these 2 Questions. 

**Q1:** Where would you say the exchange began a shift to destructive conflict.

**Q2:** if Shilpa had invited you to observe and potentially mediate the exchange, what’s an intervention you’d suggest to keep the discussion productive?

We regularly need to explain Scrum and its benefits to people outside the team - managers, executives, and other stakeholders who may be skeptical or unfamiliar. A clear, concise framing makes all the difference. Focus on benefits and not Scrum itself.

### Framing Scrum for Stakeholders

Peter Stevens offers a useful way to describe Scrum in business terms:

> Scrum is a simple, team-based framework for solving complex problems, like creating great products or taking an organization to the next level. The essence of Scrum can be applied at any level of your organization:
>
> - **Cadence** - Inspect and adapt at frequent, regular intervals.
> - **Ownership** - Solve the whole problem in a small team, from idea to done.
> - **Speed** - Help the team and the organization improve and collaborate to deliver value faster.
> - **Tangible results** - Produce in cadence something you can use, sell, or test in real life.
> - **Alignment** - Speak to one specific person for decisions about the product.
> - **Leadership** - Lead by providing guidance and support, and know when to stay out of the way.
>
> "The purpose of an agile transformation is to restructure the company to optimize for speed and value generation."
>

Notice that this framing avoids Scrum jargon (no mention of Sprints, Product Backlogs, or ceremonies). It speaks in terms stakeholders care about: speed, value, ownership, and results. When you pitch Scrum to a stakeholder, lead with their problems and show how Scrum addresses them.

### Building Your Pitch
Imagine you encounter a business stakeholder who could benefit from Scrum but is not yet convinced. You have 1-3 minutes. How do you make the case?

A few tips:
- **Start with their pain.** What problem are they struggling with? Slow delivery? Misaligned priorities? Lack of visibility into progress?
- **Connect Scrum to their problem.** Use the framing above - pick the two or three points most relevant to their situation.
- **Keep it concrete.** Instead of "we inspect and adapt," try "every two weeks the team delivers working software and gets feedback, so we catch problems early instead of six months in."
- **Avoid jargon.** If you say "Sprint Retrospective" to someone who has never heard of Scrum, you have already lost them.

### Assignment

1. Think of a real stakeholder in your organization who could benefit from Scrum or who is not yet convinced. What are their biggest concerns or pain points?
2. Write a 1-3 minute pitch tailored to that stakeholder. Focus on the benefits that matter most to them, using language they would use. Share your pitch in your personal Mural board.

Good rewrite overall - punchier and more concrete than my draft. Here's the feedback, split as asked:

**Grammar (needs fixing before publish)**

1. **Title/body mismatch**: title says "Inspect and Adapt" (verbs) but the body consistently uses "inspection" and "adaptation" (nouns). Pick one - I'd match the body: *"3.2B Diagnosing Transparency, Inspection, and Adaptation Failures"*.
2. **Subject-verb agreement**: "The team see the problem(s)" → "The team **sees**..." (collective noun, singular).
3. **Dropped word**: "they just give." → "they just give **up**."
4. **Comma splice**: "Adaptation failures are demoralizing, the team can see the problem, but they fail to act." - two independent clauses joined by only a comma. Use a colon or period: "Adaptation failures are demoralizing: the team can see the problem but fails to act."
5. **Pronoun inconsistency**: "the team can see... but **they** fail" mixes singular "team" with plural "they" - same issue as #2, pick singular throughout.
6. **"team(s)"**: the inline plural-in-parentheses ("outside of the team(s) control") reads like a placeholder you forgot to resolve, not a stylistic choice. Just write "the team's control."
7. **Missing article**: "Sprint Backlog that isn't updated." and "Daily Scrum where team members..." both need "A" like their neighbors ("A Definition of Done...", "A Retrospective..."). Right now 2 of 4 items in that list have an article and 2 don't.
8. **Missing Oxford comma** in the inspection-failures list: "...a Daily Scrum that becomes a status report to the Scrum Master **or** a Retrospective..." should be "..., or a Retrospective..." (three-item list, no comma before "or").
9. **"the 'ignored'"** doesn't parse - "called the ignored" needs "the" to modify a noun that isn't there. Something like "a Definition of Done nobody enforces" reads cleaner and drops the quote-mark issue too.

**Tone**

- The shift from my narrative paragraphs to short, punchy fragments ("Sprint Backlog that isn't updated. ... Daily Scrum where team members constantly repeat no blockers.") is a good instinct - it's snappier and more concrete, closer to how you'd talk in class. Keep it.
- But right now it's inconsistently punchy: some items are fragments, some are full sentences, some have articles, some don't. Fragments read as intentional style only when they're parallel - make all four bullets in the Transparency section the same shape ("A ___ that ___.") and it'll land as a deliberate rhythm instead of looking unproofread.
- "repeat no blockers" is a little unclear - do you mean the team keeps saying "no blockers" even when there are some? If so, quoting it ("keep saying 'no blockers'") would make the failure mode obvious at a glance.
- "Cycle Time Data" - capitalized like a Scrum artifact (Sprint Backlog, Definition of Done), but it isn't one, and elsewhere in the course (5.1-Scaling.mdx) "cycle time" is lowercase. Worth lowercasing here for consistency with the rest of the site.
- Overall tone is more direct and classroom-voice than my draft, which fits the course better - just needs a proofreading pass, it currently reads like a first-draft brain dump rather than a polished page.
